messages.subject: High test statistic when the residuals' values  are low. Problem with CFA model
parts:
Hello,

I have a problem with my CFA model. I use MLM estimator. I've already checked modification indices and added 4 additional parameters with mi values bigger than 3.84 and epc values bigger than 0.2 to the model. I've checked residuals and deleted 2 indicators  bigger than 0.1.
 
I don't understand why I have large robust test statistic = 96.281 and robust p-value = 0.000 when all the residuals' values are low now. I want to add that I tried to run the same model with WLSMV estimator (my data is ordinal). As I understand,  the siatuation was not much  better with robust test statistic = 78.147 and robust p-value =0.000.
 
How can I improve the model?
Below you can see a part of the model's output with MLM estimator, residuals for this model and fit measures:

messages.author: cf6f800b12f87d14
messages.subject: Re: High test statistic when the residuals' values are low. Problem with CFA model
parts:
Hi Iraida,

Chi-squared statistic is influenced by sample size. You have more than 1800 cases, the chi-squared test is too sensitive and will basically always be significant, no matter what model you have. In this case, you can just ignore that (but still report them later) and interpret the other fit indices. (CFI, TLI, RMSEA & SRMR).

Cheers,
Hsin-Rui Lin

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: High test statistic when the residuals' values are low. Problem with CFA model
parts: the chi-squared test is too sensitive and will basically always be significant, no matter what model you have

I object to this mischaracterization.  The chi-squared statistic is exactly as sensitive as it should be to maximize power (i.e., "sensitivity") given the chosen Type I error rate.  And if your model is exactly correct, N has no effect on the rejection rate; it will be nominal, assuming your model's assumptions are met (not just the constraints, but normality, etc.).  This is how a test statistic is supposed to behave.  You use chi-squared to assess statistical significance, not practical significance.

That being said, chi-squared can be statistically significant when there is an egregious misspecification, but also when there are many minor (arguably ignorable) misspecifications that accumulate in the single test statistic.  I agree you probably have a lot of power to detect the set of minor discrepancies you see in the matrix of standardized residuals, and I would conclude that the latter (which are standardized effect sizes, that should always accompany a test of statistical significance) indicate the degree to which the H0 of perfect fit (which you rejected) is false appears to be of little practical importance.  

I'm not trying to be overly pedantic, but this is something I have to clarify about chi-squared almost every time I review a paper using SEM.  The limitation of the chi-squared test is not the statistic's behavior, but rather how important it is to the researcher that its H0 be exactly true.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
